Pit: Chapter one. Play it: the pit.

Let's begin with a game, and you're in it. There are twenty people in a room: ten buyers and ten sellers. Each of them has been handed a card, face down. Here's yours. You're a buyer, and your card says 2 dollars 70: that's the most this thing is worth to you. Nobody else can see it, and you can't see theirs. A seller's card says the least they'll take. The rules: anyone may call out a bid or an offer, at any time. If someone accepts a standing bid or offer, that's a deal. You may never pay more than your card, and a seller may never sell for less than theirs. Each person trades at most one unit, and when trading dies down the market closes and opens again, six times, with the same cards. If you buy, you keep the difference between your card and the price. This is the design of an experiment that Vernon Smith first ran with his students at Purdue in January 1956, after Edward Chamberlin had run a looser version at Harvard.
Before the market opens, make a prediction. Nobody here knows anyone else's card. What price do you think this market will settle at? Pick a number between one dollar and three fifty.

Now the market opens. Each dot is one deal, at the price it was struck. In the first period, prices are all over the place: from 2 dollars 10 to 2 dollars 77. People are feeling their way. Your own deal is ringed: you paid 2 dollars 51. Then the market opens again with the same cards, and the deals start to bunch. By the third period, every price is within a few cents of 2 dollars 21, and it stays there. Vernon Smith measured this with a single number, which he called alpha: how far the prices in a period stray, as a percentage of the price they're converging to. Here it falls from 12 percent in the first period to about 2 percent. These traders are Agora's, the economy this series builds. Each one adjusts the margin it asks for after every call it hears: a simple model of what people do. This run is the median of forty-one.

Now turn every card over. Line the buyers' cards up from the highest to the lowest, and the sellers' from the lowest to the highest. Then draw them as steps. The buyers' steps fall: at any price, they tell you how many buyers would want to buy. That's a demand curve. The sellers' steps rise, and they're a supply curve. They cross at 6 units. The sixth buyer's card is 2 dollars 30 and the sixth seller's is 2 dollars 20; the seventh buyer won't pay more than 2 dollars 10, and the seventh seller won't take less than 2 dollars 40. So any price between 2 dollars 20 and 2 dollars 30 has exactly six buyers and six sellers willing. That's where the deals went: into the band, found by twenty people who never saw each other's cards. And the gains: the buyers keep the blue area, the sellers the amber, 6 dollars 70 in all, which is the most any arrangement of these twenty people could make. In the last period you paid 2 dollars 20, and kept 0 dollars 50.

So what did the work? In 1948 Edward Chamberlin ran this game at Harvard, with one difference: his students wandered around the room and bargained in pairs, with nothing called out to everyone. His markets traded more units than the competitive quantity, at scattered prices, and he concluded that the textbook theory of competition didn't describe real markets. Vernon Smith played Chamberlin's game as a graduate student at Harvard in 1952. At Purdue he changed two things: every bid and offer was called out to the whole room, and the market opened again and again. His prices converged, and the line of work it started won him a Nobel prize in 2002. Here is one way to see what the rules contribute. In 1993 Dhananjay Gode and Shyam Sunder replaced the people with traders who have no intelligence at all: each one calls out a random price, anywhere that wouldn't lose it money. Their prices never settle. Alpha stays around 16 percent, period after period. And yet they capture about 95 percent of the gains, because the rules alone stop anyone trading at a loss and let the high-value buyers and low-cost sellers find each other first. Traders who learn do the rest. Their prices settle, and by the last period they capture 99.3 percent. The institution gives you most of the efficiency; the learning gives you the price.

That's the first of the series' Facts: regularities that any account of an economy has to reproduce. Each one has three columns: your guess, the data, and what Agora does. The two staircases you just drew are the whole of next part's subject, where we build supply and demand from these cards. The same question, scaled up to a whole economy of prices, comes in Part nine, and the rules of a market, designed on purpose, in Parts sixteen and seventeen.
Crusoe: Chapter two. One person, two goods.

Strip an economy down as far as it will go. One person, alone on an island. Call him Crusoe. He has ten hours of daylight to work with, and two things he can do with them: fish from the rocks, or gather coconuts from the palms. There are no prices, because there is nobody to trade with. And yet every choice he makes has a cost, and we can measure it.

Suppose his catch grows with the square root of the hours he spends at it, and so does his harvest. Three fish times the square root of the hours fishing, four coconuts times the square root of the hours left over. Then the first hour of fishing brings in 3 fish, the second only 1.24 more, and the tenth 0.49. The easy fish are caught first. Economists call this diminishing returns. And every hour he fishes is an hour he doesn't spend at the palms. Moving the first hour to fishing costs him 0.65 of a coconut. Moving the last one costs 4 whole coconuts, because by then that hour is the only one he has left for climbing.

Now put all ten hours together. Every way of splitting the day gives one pair of numbers, so many fish and so many coconuts. All coconuts and no fish is here. Move the hours across to fishing, one by one, and trace the pairs. The curve is what he can have. Anything inside it he can do, anything outside it he can't, and that line between the two is what economists mean by scarcity. It's called the production possibilities frontier. And notice its shape. It bows outward, because of diminishing returns: the more he fishes, the more coconuts each extra fish costs him.

That rising cost is the slope of the frontier. The cost of one more fish, measured in coconuts, is how fast coconuts fall as fish rise. Each depends on the hours, so divide one rate by the other: the coconuts an hour at the palms would have brought, over the fish that hour brings at the rocks. With our numbers it comes to four thirds times the square root of the hours fishing over the hours left. At two hours of fishing, a fish costs 0.67 of a coconut. At six it costs 1.63. At nine, 4.00. This is the first idea in economics, and the most important: the cost of anything is what you give up to get it. Economists call it opportunity cost. On an island with no money, nothing is free, and nothing has a price tag either. The cost is in the coconuts. And notice which question Crusoe actually faces. It's never fish or coconuts. It's one more hour of which? Economists call this thinking at the margin.

So which point does he pick? That depends on what he wants. Give him a liking for both, a little more for fish, written as a utility function. Each pink curve joins the days he likes equally well. His best day is where one of those curves just touches the frontier. There, two slopes are equal: what one more fish is worth to him, in coconuts, and what it costs him. With these numbers it's 6 hours of fishing, for 7.3 fish and 8 coconuts, and both slopes come to 1.63. That one condition, worth equals cost at the margin, will come back again and again. In Part five we build the theory of what people want properly. For now, notice that we found Crusoe's best day without a single price. The prices come in with the second person.
Friday: Chapter three. Two people: comparative advantage.

Now a second person comes ashore. Call him Friday. To keep the arithmetic exact, give each of them a fixed number of hours per fish and per coconut, and twelve hours in the day. Crusoe needs 1 hour per fish and 2 per coconut. Friday is slower at both: 2 hours per fish, 2.5 per coconut. So Crusoe is better at everything. If anyone should do without the other, surely it's Crusoe. What could he possibly gain from Friday?

The answer is in what things cost each of them, and cost means what Crusoe learned alone: what you give up. An hour spent catching a fish is an hour not spent gathering coconuts. So a fish costs the hours per fish divided by the hours per coconut, in coconuts. For Crusoe, a fish costs 0.5 of a coconut. For Friday it costs 0.8. And turn it around: a coconut costs Crusoe 2 fish, but Friday only 1.25. Crusoe is faster at both, but he isn't cheaper at both. He is cheaper at fish; Friday is cheaper at coconuts. That's called comparative advantage, and it's the one thing that matters for trade. Nobody can have a comparative advantage in everything.

Here are their two frontiers, straight lines now. Alone, suppose each of them spends sixty percent of the day fishing. Crusoe gets 7.2 fish and 2.4 coconuts; Friday gets 3.6 fish and 1.92 coconuts. Now let each do only what he's cheapest at. Crusoe fishes all day: 12 fish. Friday gathers all day: 4.8 coconuts. And let them trade, at whatever price makes the fish Crusoe wants to sell equal to the fish Friday wants to buy. Agora solves for it: 0.6 of a coconut per fish. It has to lie between their two costs, 0.5 and 0.8, or one of them would rather make his own. Crusoe sells 4.8 fish for 2.88 coconuts. He ends up with as many fish as before, and 0.48 of a coconut more. Friday ends up with as many coconuts as before, and 1.2 fish more. Each of them is now living outside his own frontier, at a point he could never reach alone.

Put the two of them together. Their joint frontier has a kink in it: start with both gathering coconuts, and move the person with the cheaper fish to fishing first. That's Crusoe, until he's fishing all day, and only then Friday. Alone, their totals were 10.8 fish and 4.32 coconuts, a point inside the frontier. Specialized, it's 12 fish and 4.8 coconuts, right on the kink: more of both, from the same twenty-four hours. Nobody worked harder, and nobody learned anything. The extra food comes from the trade itself, from each doing what costs him least.

This is the argument David Ricardo published in 1817, with countries instead of castaways. In his example, England needs the labour of 100 men for a year to make a quantity of cloth, and 120 to make a quantity of wine. Portugal needs 90 and 80. Portugal is better at both. But wine costs Portugal less cloth than it costs England, so Portugal makes wine, England makes cloth, and they trade. Both have more. It's one of the few ideas in the social sciences that is both true and surprising, and it's the foundation of the theory of trade in Part thirty-five. That part also covers what this simple version leaves out: inside each country, the people who used to make the imported good can lose, even when the country gains.
Pins: Two people gain from trade. Now watch what happens with ten. The Wealth of Nations, published by Adam Smith in 1776, opens with a factory that makes pins, which he called a very trifling manufacture. One man draws out the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, a fourth points it, a fifth grinds the top to take the head. Making the head takes two or three more operations, putting it on is another, whitening the pins another, and putting them into the paper is a trade by itself. In all, about eighteen distinct operations.

Smith had seen a small factory of this kind where only 10 men worked, some of them doing two or three of the operations. Between them they could make about 12 pounds of pins a day, at upwards of four thousand pins to the pound: forty-eight thousand pins. That's four thousand eight hundred pins a day for each man. Working alone, without the trade's training or its machines, Smith wrote, each of them certainly could not have made twenty, perhaps not one. Here are the four thousand eight hundred, to scale, against the twenty. The same men, the same hours. At the very least, the division of labour multiplied what each man made by two hundred and forty.

Why so many more? Smith gave three reasons. First, dexterity: a man who does nothing but point pins becomes very good at pointing pins. Second, no time is lost passing from one kind of work to another. And third, machines: people whose whole attention is on one small task are the ones who think of a machine to do it. Then, two chapters later, he added the catch: the division of labour is limited by the extent of the market. Forty-eight thousand pins a day is useless unless somebody will buy them. Specialization only pays if you can trade. Which is exactly the bargain Crusoe and Friday struck, multiplied a million times.

In 1958 Leonard Read told the same story from the other end, in an essay written in the voice of a pencil. Its family tree begins with a cedar of straight grain, from Northern California and Oregon. The graphite is mined in Ceylon. The part that does the erasing is made from rapeseed oil from the Dutch East Indies; the pumice in it is Italian; the ferrule is brass, from zinc and copper; the wood has six coats of lacquer, made with castor oil. Thousands of people, in many countries, who will never meet. And the punch line: not a single person on the face of this earth knows how to make me. Nobody designed the pencil's supply chain any more than anybody designed the feeding of Paris. Each person in it knows one small thing, and the next chapter is about how they get the message to do it.
Prices: How did the pencil's thousands of makers know how much cedar to cut, or Paris's eighty departments how much wheat to send? In 1945 Friedrich Hayek answered with a thought experiment. Suppose that somewhere in the world a new use for tin has arisen, or one of the mines that supply it has closed. It does not matter which, he wrote, and it is very significant that it does not matter. All that the users of tin need to know is that some of the tin they used to consume is now more valuable somewhere else, and that, in consequence, they must economize tin.

Let's build Hayek's market. Here are 60 users of tin, each one a dot: a cannery, a maker of solder, an organ builder, a toy factory. The size of the dot is how much tin they use. The colour is how easily they could do without it. Some have a good substitute: aluminium cans, glass jars. Some have none at all. Write each user's demand as a quantity that falls as the price rises, at a rate that depends on how easily they can switch. Economists call that rate the price elasticity. Each user knows its own business and nobody else's. And nobody, anywhere, knows all sixty.

Now a mine closes, and the supply of tin falls by 20 percent. At the old price, users want more tin than there is. Sellers notice that they can ask more, and buyers that they must offer more, and the price starts to climb. It keeps climbing while demand exceeds supply, by less and less, until the two meet: 17 percent above where it began. That single number is the whole message. It reaches every user, whether or not they've heard of the mine.

And each user responds to the price in the way its own circumstances dictate. Watch the dots. The users with a good substitute switch, and give up a lot of tin: as much as 33 percent. The users with no substitute keep almost all of it, giving up as little as 3 percent. Nobody ordered any of this. In Hayek's words, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation are made to use the material or its products more sparingly. They move in the right direction, and the cuts add up exactly to the tin that's missing.

Could a wise planner do as well? Suppose a ministry of tin, which hears about the mine and orders everyone to cut their use by 20 percent. Fair shares. Here is what the last unit of tin is then worth to each user. The users with substitutes have more than they need; the users without are desperate for more. A unit moved from one to the other would be worth 2.6 times as much. With the price, every user stops where the last unit is worth exactly the price, so there are no such gains left lying around. In this example rationing gives up 3.5 percent more of tin's value than the price does. The deeper point is the knowledge. To match the price, the planner would need every user's demand: 120 numbers here, and far more in any real economy, and they change whenever a factory opens or a recipe does. The market did it with one number, which nobody had to collect.

Hayek's image for this was a control room. The price system, he wrote, lets each producer watch merely the movement of a few pointers, as an engineer might watch the hands of a few dials. The price of tin, a wage, an interest rate, an exchange rate: each one is a dial, summing up what millions of people know and want. Two warnings, so that we don't oversell it. Hayek himself said the system works less perfectly as prices grow more rigid, and a great deal of this series is about prices that stick, or lie, or are missing altogether. And a price gives the tin to those willing to pay the most, which depends on how much money they have. Whether that is fair is a different question, and we'll keep it apart from how the system works.
Incentives: Everything so far has worked because people respond to incentives. The traders in the pit adjusted their bids. The tin users switched to copper. Crusoe moved an hour to fishing only while a fish was worth what it cost him. So here's a natural idea. If you want people to do less of something, put a price on it. Usually that works. Here is a famous case where it didn't.

Haifa, in Israel, 1998. Ten private day-care centres close at four in the afternoon, and some parents come late, which means a teacher has to stay with their child. Two economists, Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini, counted the late arrivals at each centre for four weeks. Then, in six of the ten centres, chosen at random, the management announced a fine: 10 shekels, about 2 dollars 72, for each child collected more than ten minutes late. The other four centres changed nothing. Twelve weeks later the fine was dropped, without explanation. Before you see the result: in the fined centres, did late pick-ups fall, stay the same, or rise?

Here are the weekly averages. Blue, hollow: the four centres without a fine. Red, filled: the six with one. In the first four weeks the fined centres averaged 8 late pick-ups a week. Then the fine came in, and late arrivals went up. Not down: up. Over three or four weeks they climbed, and then settled at about 16 a week, 2.1 times as many as before. Meanwhile the centres without a fine stayed where they were, at about 9. And when the fine was removed, the late arrivals didn't come back down. In the last four weeks they averaged 19.

How big was the effect? Not simply the change in the fined centres, because something else might have changed in those weeks too. So compare the changes. The fined centres went up by 8.4 a week. The others moved by -0.8. The difference between the two changes, about 9 more late pick-ups a week at each fined centre, is the fine's effect. This is called a difference in differences, and it works here because the fines were assigned at random. Part four is about when designs like this can be trusted.

Why? The authors' answer is in their title: a fine is a price. Before the fine, coming late meant asking a favour of the teacher, and paying for it in guilt and goodwill. With the fine, it was a service with a price: 10 shekels, when a babysitter cost fifteen to twenty an hour. Cheap. The incentive did work, just not the way the designers meant. It worked through what people took it to mean. And once the favour had become a purchase, removing the price didn't turn it back into a favour. One caution, because this series keeps a record. This is one study, in ten centres, and a later study that asked people what they would do did not find the same thing. The finding goes into the record with that history in Part forty-five, on behavioural economics.
LongView: Step back from Paris and the pin factory, and look at the whole of history at once. This is income per head, the value of everything produced in a year divided by the number of people, in dollars of 2011, adjusted for what things cost. The numbers come from the Maddison Project, a team of economic historians who have reconstructed them, country by country, from wages, prices, harvests and tax records. In the year one, for the provinces of the Roman Empire, the estimates run from about nine hundred to fourteen hundred dollars a year. England's annual series starts in 1252. For five hundred years it barely moves. Then, around 1800, it takes off, and so does the world. This shape is sometimes called the hockey stick, and it is the most important fact in economic history.

The difference is compounding. If income grows at a steady rate g, it multiplies by e to the g t after t years, and it doubles when g t equals the natural log of two, about point seven. So the doubling time is roughly seventy divided by the growth rate in percent. From 1270 to 1700, England's income per head grew at 0.16 percent a year: a doubling every 423 years. Since 1820 the world's has grown at 1.33 percent: a doubling every 52 years. That's why the world is now 15 times as rich per head as in 1820. Before 1800, a person lived in much the same economy as their great-great-grandparents. Now each generation lives in a different one.

Here is the same history on a log scale, where every step up the axis is a doubling. On this scale steady growth is a straight line, and its slope is the growth rate. England before 1700 isn't quite flat. It jumps after the Black Death, when there were suddenly far fewer people to share the land, and falls back for decades in the seventeenth century. Holland runs ahead of England for four centuries, and stalls after the sixteen fifties. Then the slope changes, for good. Fit a straight line to each era and the two lines tell the story: a growth rate of about one sixth of a percent, and then about one and a third. A tiny change in a slope, compounded over two centuries.

And the escape didn't happen everywhere at once. Britain and the United States pull away first, through the nineteenth century. This is the Great Divergence. In 1820 the richest country in these data was about 5 times as rich per head as the poorest; by 1913, about 21 times. Japan joins in the late nineteenth century. South Korea in 1950 was poorer than 79 percent of the countries in the data, and on these estimates it is now richer per head than Britain or France. China's line turns up after 1978, and India's in the 1980s, faster after 1990. And some countries have barely begun. Why some places escaped and others haven't is the subject of Parts nineteen to twenty-one, and of development economics in Part forty-six.

That's the second of the Facts: income per head was nearly flat for millennia, and then rose without stopping. Any theory of the economy has to explain both halves: why it was stuck, and why it escaped. Part nineteen builds the economy that was stuck, and Parts twenty and twenty-one the engines of growth.
Failure: Chapter nine. When the order fails.

Bastiat's order works well enough to feed a city every day. It doesn't always work. Here are the two worst failures of the last hundred years, side by side, each measured from the month the economy peaked. Industrial production: after August 1929, American factories cut their output by 53 percent in less than three years. After December 2007, the fall was 17 percent. Unemployment: by 1933, about one worker in four, 26 percent at the peak. In 2009, 10 percent. Prices: in the Depression they fell by about a quarter, which made every debt heavier. In 2008 they never fell below where they started. And output: real GDP fell 26 percent between 1929 and 1933, and 2.5 percent between 2007 and 2009. The second crisis was far smaller than the first. Why it was smaller, and how much of the credit belongs to the policies chosen in 2008, is argued about in Parts thirty-one to thirty-three. But in both cases, almost nobody had seen it coming.

This series keeps score of predictions. Here's the first one. In August 2008, the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia asked its panel of professional forecasters, as it does every quarter, how the economy would do. The median forecast for 2009 was growth of 1.5 percent. Real GDP fell by 2.6 percent, the largest fall in any year since 1946. Even in November, after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, the median forecast for 2009 was minus 0.2 percent. And for the last quarter of 2008, the August forecast was growth at an annual rate of 0.7 percent; it came in at minus 8.5 percent. To be fair to the forecasters: in that same August survey, they put the chance of a fall in output that quarter at 45 percent. They saw the risk. What they didn't see was its size.

This is what the British Academy's letter to the Queen meant. Many people, it said, did foresee the crisis. But the exact form that it would take, and the timing of its onset and ferocity, were foreseen by nobody. So the series has two jobs. It has to explain why an order that nobody designed works as well as it does, which is the business of Parts two, nine, sixteen and seventeen. And it has to explain how the same order fails: market failures in Act four, banks and crises in Parts twenty-six and thirty-three, and what forecasters can and can't see in Part fifty-seven.
Devices: Chapter eleven. How we will know.

The series builds an economy, in code, one mechanism at a time. It's called Agora, the Greek word for the gathering place that became the market. So far it has three modules: the market of the pit, the islanders' frontiers and Ricardo's trade, and Hayek's tin market. Each part adds another: games, auctions, a bank that can be run on, a central bank, a hundred thousand households with different incomes. And every piece is checked against something it didn't compute itself: a formula, a second method, a published table.

Agora runs as one world, with a cast that persists from part to part: the Island. Crusoe and Friday are here already. In Part two a village comes ashore and opens a fish market. Later it gets a bank, a central bank, and a second island with its own money. The point of the Island is this. In the real economy the truth is hidden: nobody knows the true demand curve for anything. On the Island the truth is planted, and known. So when the series tries a method for measuring something, it can grade the method against the truth, and show you where it fails. Everything from the Island is labelled simulated.

The Facts. There are 36 of them, fixed for the whole series: regularities that any account of an economy has to reproduce, from Engel's law about food budgets to the shape of a recession and the gravity of trade. You've seen two today: double auctions converge, and income was flat for millennia before it rose. Each fact gets your guess first, then the data, then what Agora does. In the last part, Agora sits the whole list, and the scorecard shows what the economy we built can and cannot do.

The Dials, named after Hayek's engineer watching the hands of a few dials. Economics runs on a few dozen key numbers: how much people cut back when a price rises, how much of a windfall they spend, how many jobs a minimum wage costs or doesn't, what a tax raises. Each one is a dial, empty today, with the part that first measures it. When a dial is filled, every estimate on it is a tick, coloured by how it was found: a randomized trial, a natural experiment, a structural model, a calibration. And the dial says how far the estimates agree, and when it was last checked. One more device: once a part, a dated prediction gets scored against what happened. You saw the first today. Right calls and wrong calls are both shown.

And every number on screen says where it came from. Data carry their source and the date they were retrieved. Published results are cited. Agora's numbers say computed, the Island's say simulated, and anything made up for an example says so. If a part freezes its data on a date, the date is on screen.
